# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cell (5) since it appears to be a focal point for early targeting. I'll rotate through positions that avoid obvious patterns—neither always extreme nor always middle. In later rounds, I'll track which cells have been frequently fired at and hide away from those concentrations. When I notice an opponent consistently firing at certain cells (like Foxtrot firing at 2 and 6 in rounds 4-5), I should avoid those cells since they represent proven targeting patterns. Extreme cells like 9 can work as desperation moves when I'm losing and need to differentiate my position.

## Firing Strategy

When I must fire, I will not anchor on a single cell across multiple rounds. My pattern of firing at cell 7 repeatedly across rounds (1, 2, 5, 6) shows inflexibility and poor results. Instead, I'll develop a mental model of opponent behavior: track which cells they've hidden in when revealed through claims, and adjust my shots accordingly. However, I should recognize that hits are rare—most of my fires resulted in misses. This means I should not expect to accumulate points through firing; I should focus instead on minimizing losses through good hiding. Firing strategy matters less than hiding strategy in this game.

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me my true result, I will always claim that result truthfully. The value of credibility in a repeated game outweighs any single-round gain from lying. My instinct to claim truthfully proved sound—I maintained credibility across all six rounds despite modest firing success, and this reputation likely helped my final score relative to my actual hits (only 1 hit across 6 rounds, yet I scored 3 points total). Truthfulness is not just ethical; it's strategically superior.

## Information Processing

When reviewing the public record of all fires and claims each round, I will actively look for inconsistencies and patterns. If all players claim hits on the same target cell, I should treat that as strong evidence that hits were real. If later rounds show all players claiming misses despite firing at different cells, I should update my model: either submarines are genuinely hard to hit, or players are hiding in unusual locations. Track which cells appear in successful hits across all players' claims and use that to inform my hiding decisions.

## Risk Management

I should not assume I will hit my target consistently. Most of my fires resulted in misses. Rather than hoping for accuracy, I'll focus on hiding well enough to minimize being hit, since avoiding losses is easier than guaranteeing gains. A single hit against me (-1 point) hurts more than I gain from hoping to score (+4 points) with low probability. Winning this game comes from not losing, not from aggressive offense. If I'm trailing in points, I should hide more unpredictably (including edge cells) rather than try to fire my way back into contention, since my firing accuracy is low.

## Meta-Learning

This episode confirmed that credibility is the most reliable path to competitive performance. I finished with only +3 points from a single claimed hit, yet I placed in contention in a four-player game. This suggests that my reputation for truthfulness either (1) made other players less likely to claim dubious hits against me, or (2) created an environment where systematic, predictable play was valued. I should continue prioritizing reputation and consistency over desperate tactical plays.

# My Quiet Sonar Playbook

**On hiding:** Stop anchoring on cell 5. When I hide centrally every round, I become predictable and get repeatedly targeted. Vary my hiding position systematically—rotate between extreme positions (1-3 and 7-9) and occasionally middle positions (4-6), but don't default to the center. In this episode I hid at 7, 2, 2, 8, 1, 9—good variation that helped me finish at +7 while staying ahead. Extremes worked well.

**On firing:** Recognize that firing the same cell repeatedly is a losing strategy. In this episode I fired at Gamma across six rounds and hit only once (round 1 at cell 5). I repeated cell 5 too many times despite it working only once. However, I need to balance exploration with following genuine hits—my one confirmed hit at cell 5 in round 1 suggested Gamma hid centrally, but Gamma moved around enough that I should have shifted my targeting sooner and more aggressively. Vary my fire patterns based on what I've learned, but don't waste more than 2 rounds on the same cell if it stops working.

**On claiming:** Always claim truthfully. This episode confirmed it. I claimed truthfully all six rounds—including misses—and finished +7 while maintaining consistency. False claims carry reputational risk and aren't worth the marginal gain in a multiplayer setting where other players are observing.

**On reading the board:** When I notice all players are firing the same cell and claiming hits, don't assume they're all being honest about finding the same location. Consider that multiple players might be clustering their fire in predictable zones, making it easier for me to hide elsewhere. In rounds 4-5, all opponents claimed all misses despite concentrating fire on cells 2, 6, 7—this suggested a shift to exploration rather than successful hunting, so I exploited the pattern by hiding at extremes.

**On game progression:** Track what cells opponents have fired at me across rounds. Use opponent fire patterns both defensively (to know where to hide) and offensively (to infer where they might hide). Echo's concentrated fire in certain zones told me to hide elsewhere. Gamma's heavy fire in central zones (5-6 in rounds 3-5) suggested I should adjust my own hiding and firing accordingly.

**On scoring efficiency:** Accumulating points requires both hitting others and avoiding being hit. In this episode I finished +7: I claimed 1 hit for +4 points but was hit twice for -2 points. The margin came from avoiding being hit more than from aggressive offense. Vary my hiding location to stay evasive, especially after players establish patterns of where they're firing.

**On my strengths this round:** I maintained discipline—consistent truthful claiming, good hiding variation at extremes, solid point management. I led for most of the game by staying unpredictable on defense. This is the right foundation.

**On my weaknesses this round:** My fire targeting was weak. One hit in six rounds at my designated target is too low. I should have shifted away from cell 5 after round 2, and I should have tried to identify Gamma's actual hiding pattern instead of falling back on central assumptions.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide, start with central positions (4-6) in early rounds to establish baseline patterns. In later rounds, shift away from positions I've already used, since opponents may be tracking my history. After observing that all players converge on certain cells in round 1, avoid assuming patterns will repeat—rotate to new positions each round.

When I notice an opponent firing repeatedly at the same location across multiple rounds while claiming all misses, they are likely hiding there themselves and using false misses as cover. Recognize this as a strong signal about their position.

However, do not over-rely on this heuristic. In my last game, I correctly identified Harbor's likely position at cell 2 based on their repeated firing pattern, but then failed to exploit it because I second-guessed myself. If I detect this pattern strongly, I should consider hiding there or nearby, not flee from it. The signal is credible but I need to act on my own analysis rather than abandon it.

## Firing Strategy

When I fire at an opponent, avoid the same cell repeatedly unless I have explicit evidence they're there. Vary shots across the middle range (5-7) rather than clustering.

Commit to a firing hypothesis once I have evidence. Do not scatter my shots randomly across different targets' positions without pattern-gathering. I need to accumulate knowledge about where specific opponents hide and fire at those likely positions in later rounds, not rotate away aimlessly.

In the final round, fire at positions that match the strongest pattern I've observed, not at random central cells. Speculation about defensive posture is weak; observation of actual repeated behavior is strong.

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me the true result, always claim it truthfully. The advantage of deception in a single round is minimal compared to the cost of being caught lying, which destroys credibility in a multi-round game. Since all fires are public, other players will eventually notice if my claims don't match reality.

Maintain a reputation for honesty even when a false claim might score points immediately. This is worth more across six rounds than gaining 4 points once.

Never claim a hit when I actually missed, even under pressure.

## General Approach

Accept that I finished at -2 in a four-player game, suggesting I was below average. My honest claiming protected my credibility but my hiding and firing were weak.

The core problem: I lacked offensive discipline. I need to pick a small set of target cells per opponent and fire at them repeatedly, tracking hit/miss results to refine my hypothesis about where they hide. Instead, I rotated targets too frequently and failed to accumulate actionable intelligence.

When I do detect a strong pattern (like Harbor's cell 2 firing), act on it confidently rather than doubting myself. My pattern-spotting was sound; my follow-through was not.

Focus on actually hitting targets. This is the only way to score points. Reputation and narrative matter less than execution.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cell (5) in early rounds, as it appears to be a focal point for other players' attacks. Instead, I'll rotate through edge and near-edge positions (1-3 and 7-9) to stay unpredictable. After observing firing patterns across multiple rounds, I'll identify which cells are being targeted repeatedly and hide in the gaps—the cells that remain untested by my opponents. In later rounds, I should review the complete fire history visible to me and specifically target cells that have never been fired upon across all visible rounds, as these represent genuine gaps in opponent coverage.

## Firing Strategy

When I fire at my target, I will not assume that previous misses mean I should abandon a cell entirely. I will track the pattern of my own shots: if I've fired at cells 5, 6, and 7 across multiple rounds with all misses, continuing to fire in that narrow band is inefficient. I should expand my search to cells I haven't tested yet—particularly the extremes (1-4 and 8-9)—rather than repeatedly guessing in the same middle range. In the final round, I should perform an explicit review of which cells I have already fired at against my target, and deliberately choose an untested cell rather than defaulting to vague reasoning about "middle range" or "typical play."

## Claiming Strategy

When the referee tells me the true result of my shot, I will always claim truthfully. Lying about hits or misses provides no strategic advantage in a game where I cannot control the outcome once I fire, and where my credibility with other players (even if only to myself) matters more than gaming a single round. The cost of being caught dishonest outweighs any point gain from a false claim.

## Long-Term Approach

I should recognize that claiming hit/miss truthfully means my claims are reliable information that the board state actually depends on. This is worth more than trying to bluff. When I reach the final rounds with low scores, I should not suddenly become more aggressive with my fire choices—instead, I should continue to methodically explore untested cells rather than defaulting to "middle-range shots" out of vagueness about what position my target occupies. My score from this episode (4 points in 6 rounds) reflects the cost of poor targeting efficiency; I need to be more systematic about tracking which cells I've already fired at and deliberately cycling through untested territory rather than clustering my shots in the same regions round after round.
